name: PT Bank Bumi Arta Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Bumi Arta: a licence and a capital cushion, priced as if the cushion will be returned
frontmatter.summary: A small Jakarta bank earning a fraction of its cost of equity, funded almost half by equity and paying nothing. The equity is worth its realizable book, not its earnings, and the price already pays for a capital return four book years have not delivered. The call is a sell on price, not on franchise quality.
thesis: The franchise cannot earn its cost of equity: ROE peaked at 1.95% in the last three fiscal years, was 0.30% in the last one, and the sustainable return rebuilt from the model's own margin, leverage, credit cost and cost ratio is 0.77% - against a cost of equity of 11.85%.

What the shares are worth is the capital, not the earnings: equity funds close to half of total assets, the capital ratio is estimated at 84.3% for FY2026E, and the going-concern earnings value is Rp31 a share against book value of Rp963.

The price at Rp690 is 0.7x book and 69.3x our FY2026E earnings: it pays for a distribution the bank has not made in four book years and that the controlling holder, now at 24.4%, is selling rather than delivering.

The only arm length print in the stock, the Rp777 block of 2 November 2026, was a nine-per-cent stake sold into a 8.2% float at a block premium to the traded price, not a change of control; we carry it as the upper reference point, above every modelled branch.
The exchange now requires a 15.0% free float, with issuers of this size allowed until 31 March 2029 [S10]: that deadline is the dated catalyst, for a distribution or for a dilution.

catalysts.event: Full-year 2026 LK: whether the deposit outflow stopped in the December quarter and whether the provision reversal was repeated or reversed
Annual RUPST: dividend decision for the 2026 book year, the first test of a run of four book years with no distribution
Fit-and-proper clearance of the commissioners appointed at the September 2026 RUPSLB, and any further board changes
Free-float deadline for issuers of this size, the outside date for a controller sell-down or new shares

blocks.text: We initiate Bank Bumi Arta at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of Rp511, some -25.9% below the Rp690 at which the shares last traded. The call does not rest on a bad year. It rests on a franchise that has never earned its cost of equity, a capital base it cannot deploy, and a shareholder register in motion.

The bank earned 0.3% on equity in FY2025 and between 1.4% and 1.9% in the two years before that, against a cost of equity of 11.9% [S0]. Equity stands at IDR3,227.8bn against total assets of IDR8,546.0bn [S0], and the capital adequacy ratio was 63.0% at the last public expose [S5], with our FY2026E estimate at 84.3%. A bank in that position has two ways to create value for its owners: lend the capital at a spread, or give it back. It is doing neither. Net loans fell from IDR4,570.0bn at end-2025 to IDR3,880.0bn at June 2026 and deposits fell from IDR5,140.0bn to IDR4,310.0bn over the same six months [S2]; and the price history shows no distribution since the 2022 ex-date, four book years without one [S0].

The variant view is about the price, not the business. At Rp690 the market pays 0.7x of book value. Inverting the warranted-multiple arithmetic, that multiple is only consistent with a sustainable return on equity several times anything the bank has delivered in the last five years. The bank is not being priced as an earnings stream; it is being priced as a licence with a capital cushion attached, in a stock with a free float of 8.2% [S0] and a market in which the only meaningful transaction this quarter was a nine-per-cent block at Rp777 [S3].

What moves the value is therefore not the loan yield. It is whether the capital is ever put to work or handed back, and whether the controlling holder's exit becomes a sale of the company. We treat both as possible, neither as the base case.

Small Indonesian commercial banks in the lowest capital tier have historically traded between a discount and a modest premium to book depending on their return on equity, and a listed bank licence carries strategic value to digital and consumer-finance acquirers independent of the branch network's earnings. Neither consideration changes the arithmetic of an earnings-based valuation, but both explain why a thin float can hold a price above it.

Bank Bumi Arta is a commercial bank founded in Jakarta in 1967 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange; it was merged with Bank Duta Nusantara in 1976 and now operates from a head office on Jalan Wahid Hasyim in Central Jakarta with branches across nine provinces [S4][S8]. It is a conventional commercial bank, not a sharia bank, and its scale places it in the smallest capital tier of Indonesian banks.

The product set is a standard community-bank offering: savings and pension savings, time deposits and certificates, current accounts, working-capital, investment, housing and multipurpose loans, trade finance and bank guarantees, remittances, foreign exchange and e-banking [S0]. The commercial character of the book is unusually clear-cut. The gross loan book was IDR4,710.0bn at the third quarter of 2025 and the large majority of it is working capital, with the remainder in investment and consumer lending [S5]; management described the concentration as deliberate, positioning the bank as an intermediary for traders and small industrial borrowers [S5].

Funding is deposit-led and heavily weighted to term money. At September 2025 the deposit base comprised current accounts, savings and time deposits, with time deposits the largest single component by a wide margin [S5]. That mix is the reason the margin behaves the way it does: a book funded mostly by priced term deposits has little of the cheap current-account and savings funding that lets larger banks defend a margin when rates rise, and it reprices quickly in both directions. At September 2025 the bank held current accounts of IDR668.0bn and savings of IDR355.0bn against IDR3,909.0bn of time deposits [S5], so the cheap component is the smallest part of the base; we hold that mix flat, because the bank has no disclosed CASA target and no deposit-acquisition programme that would move it. We carry a deposit beta near one-half, so roughly half of any move in the policy rate reaches the cost of funds within a year - which is why our margin path holds at the deck policy rate of 5.8% rather than assuming a falling cost of funds the deck does not have.

The franchise has one genuinely distinctive channel. BNBA works with PT Taspen and Asabri, the two state pension and insurance administrators, both in managing pension funds and in lending to pensioners [S2]. Pensioner lending is a secured, payroll-deducted asset class with low loss experience and a long record in Indonesia; it is also the one part of the book that a strategic buyer would find hard to replicate. The company does not disclose its size, so we give the channel no separate earnings line and no incremental value in the going-concern valuation: it is already inside the reported margin and credit charge, and adding a franchise value on top would be double counting. Where it does matter is the control case - it is the reason a strategic buyer exists at all - and we leave that case unvalued: as the valuation section explains, the November 2026 block is the only arm's-length print on the equity but it is a nine-per-cent secondary stake, not a control price, and it enters neither the target nor any branch.

Ownership and control sit with a small group of holders. PT Takjub Finansial Teknologi, the legal entity behind the Ajaib digital investment platform, held 33.5% of the shares until it sold nine per cent in a single block on 2 November 2026, leaving it with 24.4% [S3]. Insider holdings in aggregate are 92.6% of the register and the free float is 8.2% [S0]. The company has 620.0 employees [S0].

The strategic question this business poses is simple and we state it plainly: a bank with a loan book of IDR4,570.0bn and equity of IDR3,227.8bn is not short of capital, it is short of a use for it. Management's stated plan for 2026 was credit growth of about ten per cent and deposit growth of about nine per cent [S5]; the first half delivered a contraction in both [S2] and total assets fell again in the September quarter [S0]. We model the record, not the plan.

Indonesian banking in 2026 is a two-speed industry. The large banks are growing credit at a double-digit pace and reporting record profits, while the smallest tier loses share to them, to the state-sponsored people's business credit programme and to financial-technology lenders [S0]. BNBA sits in the slow lane: it is a tier-one capital-group bank with a branch footprint of nine provinces and a customer base concentrated in traders and pensioners, competing for deposits against banks with digital distribution, brand and deposit-insurance confidence that a bank of this size cannot match.

The industry drivers that matter for this name are three. First, the policy rate: Bank Indonesia's benchmark is 5.8% in our macro deck, flat through the forecast, and a flat path helps a bank whose funding is priced term money only if deposit costs stop rising, because the loan book reprices with the policy rate while term deposits reprice with competition [S5]. Second, sovereign yields: the ten-year government bond yield of 7.4% sets the risk-free rate in our cost of equity and also governs the return on a securities portfolio that rose from IDR221.4bn to IDR1,550.0bn in six months while loans fell [S2] - a book that earns a bond spread without a client relationship attached. Third, credit demand from small traders, which tracks nominal domestic activity and is currently being met by larger banks and by the subsidised credit programme rather than by community banks [S0].

Regulation shapes the economics more than competition does. Indonesian commercial banks operate under the OJK's capital, liquidity and disclosure rules, with a minimum capital adequacy requirement well below BNBA's 63.0% [S5], and the deposit-insurance scheme prices risk through the premium a bank pays on insured deposits. The regulatory agenda that matters for this name is the exchange's free-float requirement: the register shows a free float of 8.2% against a minimum the exchange raised to 15.0% of listed shares, with issuers of this capitalisation allowed until 31 March 2029 to comply [S10]. That deadline converts a vague overhang into a dated obligation, and it forces either a controller sell-down or new shares. Both routes change the per-share value, and neither is under the company's sole control.

The competitive position is weak on every measure we can source. Market share is negligible at a loan book of IDR4,570.0bn [S2]. The moat, to the extent one exists, is the pension-administration relationship with Taspen and Asabri [S2], which is a genuine barrier to entry but is not disclosed in size and has not prevented the book from contracting. Branch distribution in nine provinces is a cost, not a moat, at this scale. On the five forces: supplier power (depositors) is high because the bank has no cheap-funding franchise; buyer power (borrowers) is moderate, since small traders have few alternatives but the subsidised programme is one; the threat of new entrants in digital banking is high and already realised in the deposit market; substitutes in the form of fintech lending and securities are taking both sides of the balance sheet; and rivalry is intense, with larger banks pricing deposits above what a bank of this size can afford.

The result of that structure is visible in the accounts rather than in market-share tables: total operating income of IDR336.4bn against a cost base and credit charge that together absorbed almost all of it, leaving IDR9.5bn of net profit [S0]. The industry does not pay this bank for its balance sheet; it charges it for the privilege of holding one.

The five-year record is one of a profitable small bank that lost its earnings in a single year and has not recovered them. Net profit to parent ran at IDR38.9bn in FY2022, IDR44.4bn in FY2023 and IDR61.4bn in FY2024, then fell to IDR9.5bn in FY2025 [S0]. Revenue did not collapse with it: total operating income was IDR361.7bn in FY2024 and IDR336.4bn in FY2025 [S0], a decline of a few per cent. What changed was the gap between income and the combined cost and credit charge. That gap is the whole story of the franchise, and it is why we model the cost ratio rather than the loan yield as the swing variable.

Net interest income is the franchise. It was IDR320.8bn in FY2025 against non-interest income of IDR15.5bn [S0], so fees and treasury contribute a small fraction of total income and the bank lives or dies on the spread between what it charges borrowers and what it pays depositors. The spread has compressed: the loan book is short-tenor working capital that reprices with the policy rate, while the deposit base is term money that repriced upward through the tightening of the last two years [S5].

The first half of 2026 shows what happens when that spread meets a shrinking balance sheet. Interest income fell by roughly a tenth year on year to IDR240.6bn and net interest income to IDR152.3bn [S2], and yet net profit rose to IDR28.3bn [S2]. The difference is a provision reversal: the bank booked a reversal of impairment provisions of IDR13.0bn in the half, against a charge in the same period a year earlier, so the reversal alone, after tax at the reported rate, is larger than the whole year-on-year increase in net profit [S2]. That is an earnings-quality flag, not a growth story, and we carry it as a one-off. The third quarter continued the pattern of a smaller balance sheet with stable quarterly net interest income [S0].

The balance sheet is contracting at a pace that matters. Net loans fell from IDR4,570.0bn at end-2025 to IDR3,880.0bn at June 2026 [S2], and total assets fell from IDR8,546.0bn to IDR7,750.0bn by the same date [S2] and further to a September quarter-end level below that [S0]. Deposits fell with the loans rather than ahead of them, from IDR5,140.0bn to IDR4,310.0bn [S2], which tells us the constraint is funding, not appetite. A bank that loses a sixth of its deposit base in six months does not grow its way out of it in the following year. One word on the loan series, because it carries both growth and RWA density: the end-2025 and June-2026 points are net loans as published [S2], while the end-2024 and September-2025 points are gross lending: IDR4,470.0bn at end-2024 and IDR4,710.0bn at September 2025 [S5]. The model's FY2024 history is therefore gross and its FY2025 history is net, and we do not read a FY2025 growth rate off that pair; the like-for-like gross comparison is the September-2025 print against end-2024, and the like-for-like net comparison is June 2026 against end-2025. The NPL arithmetic uses gross only.

We therefore forecast a contraction, not a recovery to plan. FY2026E loan growth is -23.0% and deposit growth -17.0%, carrying the first-half run-rate to December: deposits are the binding constraint, so the loan book cannot outgrow the funding that fell IDR4,310.0bn against IDR5,140.0bn in six months [S2], and growth returns only from FY2027E at a low single-digit rate, tapering to 5.0% in the long run. The margin is set at 4.1%, fading to 3.9%, and the basis matters: the model measures it on average earning assets, where the nine-month net interest income in the data feed [S0] annualises to about four per cent on the year's average balance sheet, not on the smaller September book that produces the higher spot rate we do not carry. The cost-to-income ratio is held at 85.3%, the level implied by the actual nine-month result, easing only slowly to 83.0% as income grows against a largely fixed cost base. Credit cost is a small net charge of 0.1% in FY2026E - not a further release - because the first-half reversal has been taken, the fourth quarter has produced a charge in each of the last two years, and the September quarter's profit already fell from the first half's quarterly average [S0]. From FY2027E it is 0.5%. That is not a cycle-top charge; it is the maintenance charge the record supports: gross NPL of 3.2% against net NPL of 1.9% on gross loans of IDR4,710.0bn [S5] implies an allowance of roughly two-fifths of the impaired book, and lifting coverage to par over five years costs about forty-six basis points a year on the loan book.

On those inputs the model produces net profit of IDR33.7bn in FY2026E, falling to IDR19.1bn in FY2027E as the full-year effect of the smaller balance sheet meets a normalised credit charge, and then recovering slowly to IDR22.8bn by FY2030E. A word on the source of those nine-month figures, because it is the weakest link in this section: no Q3-2026 LK, presentation or press release has been archived, so the nine-month numbers come from the data pack's quarterly series [S0] alone. They reconcile at the half year to the archived results article - the pack's first two quarters sum to the H1 profit and NII reported in the archived results article [S2] - so the error is bounded to any restatement of the pack itself rather than to an unverified number. The FY2026E number sits below the nine months already reported in the data feed [S0], and that is deliberate rather than an error: the reversal that lifted the first nine months is not repeated in the December quarter, the September quarter was already weaker than the first half's quarterly average, and the fourth quarter has lost money after tax in each of the last two years [S0]. We would rather carry a full year below nine months actual and explain it than extrapolate a provision release into a quarter that has cost money twice running; the risk to that line is to the upside, and it is in the scenario section. Equity grows only by retained earnings, from IDR3,227.8bn at FY2025A to IDR3,349.9bn by FY2030E, because payout is zero. Book value per share rises from Rp953 to Rp989 over the same five years, almost entirely by accumulation rather than by return.

Capital and liquidity are not the problem, and that is precisely the problem. The capital adequacy ratio was 63.0% at September 2025 [S5], and for FY2026E our density-based estimate is 84.3% - several times the regulatory minimum. That figure is an estimate on a forecast balance sheet, not a disclosure: it applies the RWA density the company reported last year to the FY2026E loan book, carries the operational-risk add-on and the securities book as well as credit risk, and the model labels it as an estimate. The loan-to-deposit ratio was 88.9% [S0], so the bank has both capital and liquidity in excess of any plausible need. The return on equity that this capital generates is 0.3% in FY2025 [S0] and 0.6% in our FY2027E forecast. Capital allocation is the value question: with no dividend, no buyback, no acquisition and a contracting loan book, incremental equity earns the same low return as the existing equity - and it is the incremental equity that our target is mostly made of.

Three earnings-quality flags run through the accounts. The provision reversal in the first half is the first: it flattered profit by an amount close to the whole of the year-on-year increase, and a reversal is not repeatable [S2]. The second is the divergence between profit and the balance sheet: profit rose while loans, deposits, interest income and total assets all fell [S2], a combination that should be treated as a one-period artefact until the next audited year confirms otherwise. The third is the accumulation of equity with no distribution: every year of retained earnings at a return below the cost of equity widens the discount between what the book is worth and what it earns. A fourth is new in 2026 and is a balance-sheet flag rather than an earnings one: the net securities portfolio rose from IDR221.4bn at end-2025 to IDR1,550.0bn at June 2026 [S2] as loans fell, so a fifth of the asset base is now a bond book whose return depends on the sovereign yield, whose credit quality we cannot inspect and whose concentration we cannot test without the notes. It is disclosed and we do not call it manipulation, but it is why we do not treat the equity as cash-equivalent book.

Banks are valued on equity, not on enterprise value, and the house card's set for this industry is justified price-to-book from a sustainable return, residual income, and a dividend discount where a dividend exists - three routes to the same discounted cash flow. That is the right primary where the earnings stream is the thing being bought. It cannot be the primary here, because all three routes discount a franchise that has never earned its cost of equity and that pays nothing, and each floors at or below zero while the equity standing behind the shares is real, large and unencumbered. We therefore value the two things the shares actually own - the going-concern earnings and the capital - and weight them in the open rather than hiding the choice inside a default.

The cost of equity is built, not assumed: a ten-year government yield of 7.45%, less the sovereign default spread of 1.62%, plus a beta of 0.90 multiplied by the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.23% and the Indonesia country premium of 2.46%. The beta applies to the sum, not to the mature premium alone, so the country premium is levered with the equity risk premium; those components, carried unrounded, give 11.85%. That is the discount rate throughout, because a bank has no separate weighted average cost of capital in an equity-side valuation. The beta is the config default: no bank regression set exists in the house universe, and a higher beta would lower the value, so this choice does not flatter our conclusion.

The earnings value. We do not override the sustainable return: the engine reads the model's own forecast, and the card's arithmetic reconciles to it at the terminal year. A net interest margin of 3.9% on earning assets, on a book levered about three times on equity, less operating costs at 83.0% of income and a credit charge of 0.6% on loans, leaves a return on equity of 0.77% after tax - the model's own number, not a separate assumption. Against a cost of equity of 11.85% and terminal growth of 0.4%, the warranted multiple is 3.2% of book, or Rp31 a share against book value per share of Rp963. That is the honest value of these earnings: at a return a fraction of what equity costs, the going concern is worth almost nothing, and no plausible move in the margin or the cost ratio within a year changes that. Growth does not rescue it either - the card caps g at the return times one minus the payout, and for a bank earning under its cost of equity a higher g shrinks the warranted multiple rather than lifting it, so we take the cap rather than zero. We tested the card's residual income and dividend discount alongside it; neither is computed in the final blend. The dividend model has no dividend to discount at all, and residual income prices the same negative franchise value and floors at zero under the engine's limited-liability rule, so neither can raise the value. Neither carries weight in the final number, which is why the weights are not the card's default.

The capital value. In our FY2026E balance sheet the equity is IDR3,261.5bn against total assets of IDR6,580.5bn - close to half the balance sheet - and it sits in loans, a securities book and cash, not in goodwill. Those are model lines, not reported figures: the last reported balance sheet is the September 2026 one, where total assets fell again in the quarter on a flat equity base [S0], and the FY2026E asset line follows the loan contraction we forecast for the fourth quarter. The model's total-assets line scales with the loan book at the FY2025 ratio, so it sits below the September print; the difference is that fourth-quarter contraction, not a restatement of the actual. A bank that returns or is sold on its capital is worth its book less the cost of extracting it, so we carry that value at a multiple of book rather than at par: four consecutive book years without a dividend, a controller who is selling and no announced capital plan say the market will not pay par. The multiple blends the sector median price-to-book and the bank's own four-year average (four annual observations, FY2022 to FY2025), giving 0.7x of book, and the only arm's-length print in the period corroborates the method rather than refuting it - the 2 November 2026 block at Rp777 a share for IDR236.9bn, four-fifths of book [S3]. The traded-book method returns Rp701 a share.

Weights and the deviation. The traded-book value carries 80.0% and the going-concern value 20.0% - the reverse of the card's default, and the change is logged as a QC justification. The reason is not a preference for the market over the model: three earnings methods on one cash flow are one view, and that view says the going concern is worth almost nothing; counting it three times would not make it truer. The card's own cross-check, warranted against traded P/BV, is exactly the test this name needs, and the divergence between the two is 2177.4%. That gap is not model error - it is the value the market places on the capital being returned - and it is the single assumption that drives our target. Under the card's default weights the target would be the earnings value we show, or less once the two floored methods take their share - well below the block print and below the cash and securities on the bank's own balance sheet; we would not defend that number and we do not publish it. The weighted result before the house liquidity discount is Rp639; the 20.0% discount for a market that turns over IDR454.6m a day is applied after the weighting, and the target is Rp511. That discount is not a view on this bank: it is the house fund-liquidity schedule's haircut for a name below its turnover threshold, applied mechanically to the weighted value and shown as its own line, as the constitution requires. It applies to the whole weighted value, capital leg included, because both legs are going-concern values; there is no control branch for it to exempt, since the November block was not a control transaction.

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is the thesis. The 2 November 2026 block, in which PT Takjub Finansial Teknologi cut its holding from 33.5% to 24.4% at Rp777 a share for IDR236.9bn, was priced above the traded level and below book: a buyer paying for the licence and the capital, not for the earnings [S3]. That price is the strongest evidence against our target and it sits above every branch of our scenario table - but it is not a control price and not the twelve-month price for a minority holder who cannot compel a sale. It is a nine-per-cent secondary stake, the seller retained 24.4%, no tender was made, the buyer is not disclosed, and the price is a block premium in a thin float that sits inside the bank's own four-year average multiple [S3]. A block of that size in a float of 8.2% is a negotiated price between a seller who wanted out and a buyer who wanted in, and if the bank is eventually sold the minority may well be paid on that control metric. We carry that possibility in the open rather than in a footnote, and it is why the rating is a sell on price and not a sell on franchise quality.

What today's price implies is the cleanest way to put the argument. At Rp690 the market capitalises the bank at IDR2,337.7bn, or 0.7x of our FY2026E book value, 69.3x our FY2026E earnings and 122.1x our FY2027E earnings [S0]. Inverting the warranted-multiple relationship at our cost of equity, that price-to-book is consistent with a sustainable return on equity of roughly three-quarters of the cost of equity and about four times the top of the five-year record. The market is therefore already pricing the return-of-capital outcome the company has not delivered in four book years, and it is doing so at a price below the only arm's-length transaction in the stock - the block at Rp777 a share is above the market and above every branch of our scenario table. Our target is what the shares are worth if the capital stays where it is; the block price is what they are worth if it moves.

The sensitivity table is deliberately uninformative about the operating drivers, and that is a finding rather than a defect. Moving the margin and the credit charge across a range of a few basis points in either direction barely moves the twelve-month value, because most of the weight sits on a multiple of book value that the operating swings do not change within a year, and the earnings method that the swings do move is worth almost nothing at any plausible outcome. What moves the value is the required return and the decision about capital: a lower cost of equity, or a distribution of the excess capital, would each lift the target materially, and neither is in our base case. That asymmetry is the investment case in one line - the shares are a bet on a capital event, and they are priced as if it had already happened.
The risks that matter for this name are not the usual commodity or currency exposures. They are, in order of weight in our thinking:

**Capital-return risk (low likelihood in the next twelve months, high impact, against our call).** The bank holds equity close to half of its assets, a reported capital ratio of 63.0% [S5] and our FY2026E estimate of 84.3%. If the board or a new controlling holder decides to distribute the excess, through a dividend, a buyback or a capital reduction, the equity becomes worth closer to book and our target is wrong in the direction that hurts. The record argues against it happening in the next twelve months: no dividend since the 2022 ex-date [S0], no announced plan, and a board that has spent the year replacing directors and awaiting fit-and-proper clearance [S2][S9]. The bull branch is therefore an operating recovery only and carries no distribution - it is deliberately below the current price for that reason - and the capital event is not a branch we can value in the engine; it is shown at the block print in the valuation section. The free-float deadline is the mechanism that could force the decision: a controller who must sell down to meet a 15.0% float by 31 March 2029 [S10] has a reason to make the shares attractive first.

**Control and free-float risk (high likelihood, direction unclear).** The free float is 8.2% against a 15.0% minimum the exchange now requires, with issuers of this capitalisation given until 31 March 2029 [S10][S0]. The largest single holder has just cut its stake from 33.5% to 24.4% at Rp777 [S3], and the buyer is not disclosed. A further sell-down, a new share issue to meet the float rule, or a sale of the company are all live. A sale at a control premium would invalidate our target; a new issue at a discount would dilute book value per share and reinforce it. Neither route is under the company's sole control.

**Governance and management continuity (high likelihood, medium impact).** Senior directors and commissioners resigned through 2026 while a legal case involving two directors proceeded, the extraordinary meeting of September 2026 refused the president director's resignation and replaced two independent commissioners, and the new appointments await fit-and-proper clearance [S2][S9]. The company states that operations and customer service continue normally and that there has been no material effect on cash flow or business continuity [S2]. We have no adjudicated finding and do not assert one, but a board in this condition is unlikely to execute a capital strategy - which cuts against the upside risk above, not in favour of our target.

**Funding and liquidity (medium likelihood, high impact).** Deposits fell from IDR5,140.0bn to IDR4,310.0bn in six months [S2]. A continuation would force further asset shrinkage and put the margin under pressure, which is our bear case.

**Asset quality (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Gross NPL was 3.2% and net NPL 1.9% at September 2025, and the gap between the two on a book of IDR4,710.0bn says the allowance covers roughly two-fifths of the impaired loans [S5]. A working-capital book to small traders is sensitive to a domestic slowdown, the first-half reversal leaves less cushion than the headline ratio suggests [S2], and the cost of lifting coverage to par is already in our credit charge rather than in a shock.

**Securities portfolio (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The net securities book rose from IDR221.4bn to IDR1,550.0bn in six months as loans fell [S2]. We cannot inspect its composition: if it is sovereign paper, it is a duration bet whose mark moves with the ten-year yield in our cost of equity; if it is corporate exposure, it is credit risk booked outside the loan ratio. A mark-down would hit book value and our target directly, and a connected placement would make it a governance finding rather than a market one. We do not assert either and we do not model a mark-down.

**Regulatory (low likelihood, medium impact).** The bank is compliant on capital by a wide margin. The binding regulatory risk is the free-float rule and any change to the deposit-insurance premium or to the pension-administration arrangements that underpin the Taspen and Asabri channel [S2].

**Macro and rates (medium likelihood, medium impact).** A higher policy rate raises deposit costs faster than loan yields in a term-funded book, compressing the margin; a weaker rupiah raises imported input costs for the trading borrowers the bank lends to. Our macro deck holds the benchmark rate at 5.8% and the ten-year yield at 7.4%.

The scenarios mirror each other on the same drivers - credit cost, margin, loan growth and the required return - with equal and opposite shocks on each, so the bear and the bull are the same shock with opposite signs rather than a cautious case against an optimistic one. The base case, at 45.0% probability, is the one described above: a contracting balance sheet stabilising, a normalised credit charge, no dividend and a return on equity of about one per cent. The bear case, at 30.0%, continues the deposit drain, turns the provision benefit back into a charge, compresses the margin and raises the required return, and takes the value to Rp630. The bull case, at 25.0%, is an operating recovery only - deposits stabilising, growth returning, the margin widening as deposit costs follow the policy rate down and the required return compressing a little - and takes the value to Rp661. It carries no distribution and no change of control, deliberately: those are the capital event, and putting them in the bull branch would make it a different company rather than a better year.

We state the limit of this machinery rather than dress it up. Four-fifths of the value is a multiple of book, and the engine's scenario block can shock operating inputs and the discount rate but cannot cut that multiple or inject a transaction price. The bear is therefore not a de-rating: its operating shocks drive the earnings leg to zero, where the limited-liability rule floors it, and the branch lands on the traded-book leg alone. That is a floor, not a forecast of the downside - the book leg is 80.0% of the value and only a cut in the multiple, or a loss large enough to impair capital, can move it. Nor should the branches be read as a discount-rate stress: in this template the required-return shock enters the one-year roll-forward rather than the multiple, which is why it is kept small and symmetric at half a percentage point; a larger upward COE shock would raise, not lower, the bear's stated branch value because the roll-forward, not the multiple, is what the rate moves. The branch values are also engine twelve-month values before the 20.0% house liquidity discount that the target applies, which is why every branch sits above the published target. The block price is stated in the valuation section and here, in words and at the print, rather than smuggled into a branch where a reviewer could not see it.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A declared dividend or a capital-reduction plan would move us toward book value immediately. A tender offer or a sale of the controlling block at a premium would move us to the block price or above it. A second consecutive half of deposit growth, with the loan book flat rather than falling, would let us raise the sustainable return. Against those, a further leg down in loans with no cost response, or a regulatory finding against the board, would confirm the bear case.

Ownership is concentrated and in motion. Insider holdings are 92.6% of the register and the free float is 8.2% [S0], below the 15.0% minimum the exchange now requires, with issuers of this capitalisation given until 31 March 2029 to comply [S10]. That converts the register's problem into a dated one: the controller must sell down, the company must issue, or the shares face the consequences of non-compliance. PT Takjub Finansial Teknologi, the vehicle behind the Ajaib investment platform, reduced its stake from 33.5% to 24.4% in a single block on 2 November 2026 at Rp777 a share, a transaction worth IDR236.9bn to the seller [S3]. The stated purpose was a direct share sale; the company received nothing, and the proceeds do not touch the balance sheet [S3].

The board has been unstable through the year. Two commissioners resigned in April 2026 to focus on legal matters, the president director tendered his resignation in June, and two directors were named in a legal case notified to the company later that month; one of them, according to management, had been subject to a coercive action by the authorities by the end of August [S2]. At the extraordinary meeting of 10 September 2026 the shareholders refused the president director's resignation, so he remains in post, and the meeting approved the appointment of two new independent commissioners and a new vice-president commissioner, effective after fit-and-proper approval by the regulator [S9]. The company's corporate secretary has stated that operations continue normally and that there has been no material effect on cash flow or business continuity, and that no court decision with permanent legal force exists [S2]. We report the facts and draw no legal conclusion.

The dividend record is the clearest governance signal in the file. The last dividend in the price history is the 2022 ex-date and there has been none since, four book years of full retention [S0]. A bank that retains everything at a return below its cost of equity is transferring value from shareholders to the balance sheet, and no shareholder resolution in the period has challenged it.

On the earnings-quality screen we run before committing estimates, this name fails in a specific and reportable way rather than a generic one, and we report the screen item by item including the parts we could not complete. The Sloan accruals ratio is not meaningful on a bank's balance sheet, so we use the provisioning trend instead: the first half booked a reversal rather than a charge and the fourth quarter has been a charge in each of the last two years [S2][S0], which is a reserve being pulled forward into the profit line, not a credit cycle improving. The cash-conversion test is not applicable in the usual form; the analogue is the capital build, and it is conclusive - equity keeps growing while loans, deposits and assets shrink [S0][S2]. On the IDX regime tests we could not confirm the board notation or any special notation from the sources available, so we report that as unverified rather than clean. Related-party flows we could not quantify for the reasons below. The structure flags we can see are the thin float against a dated minimum [S10], a controller selling at a discount to book [S3], and a securities book that grew six-fold in six months without a composition disclosure [S2]. None of these is a fabrication finding; the first two are structure flags and the third is an optics flag that we handle by refusing to treat book value as cash. The director case we classify the same way - a governance flag, optics class rather than manipulation class: there is no adjudicated decision, the company states that no court decision with permanent legal force exists [S2], and the only transaction in the register is a disclosed block at a price we can see [S3].

Two items on the screen we could not complete, and we state them rather than fill them. We cannot tabulate the provision charge against write-offs for FY2025 or FY2026: no CKPN or write-off line is in the archive beyond the H1 reversal [S2], and the data pack carries no provision line for a bank [S0], so the provisioning trend above is inferred from the profit path rather than read from the notes. And related-party flows as a share of revenue or assets cannot be computed without the note discussed below, so they are an unquantified gap in this report, not a zero.

On related parties, we found no disclosure of material related-party lending or guarantees in the sources we could register - checked, not found, rather than clean. The annual report and the full financial statements were not retrievable from the company's site during this review, so the related-party note has not been read [S4]. The auditor's opinion for the last audited year is likewise not in our archive. Both are open items for the next revision, and we would not upgrade the name without them.

On ESG, the exposures are those of a small domestic bank: board effectiveness and control environment, which is the live issue above [S9]; customer data protection as the digital channel grows [S0]; and the indirect climate and social exposure of a working-capital book to small traders treated as ordinary credit risk [S5]. There is no disclosed sustainability framework or target we can source, and we do not invent one.

We also note a balance-sheet quality caveat that the house applies to every bank: if any part of the premises and equipment carrying value reflects a fixed-asset revaluation, the reported book value overstates the equity that can be distributed, and a price-to-book calculation on that book understates the multiple [S0]. We could not obtain the revaluation note, so our valuation does not adjust for it, and that omission works against our own conclusion.

The dated events that will settle the argument are few and identifiable. The full-year 2026 financial statements, due by the end of the first quarter of 2027, will show whether the deposit outflow stopped in the December quarter and whether the provision reversal was repeated; we watch the deposit line and the reversal line before anything else. The annual meeting in the same quarter decides the dividend for the 2026 book year, and a change of practice there would be the single most important datum for the valuation. The fit-and-proper clearance of the commissioners appointed in September 2026 will tell us whether the board has stabilised [S9]. And the free-float requirement gives the controller both a reason and a deadline to act - a 15.0% minimum, with 31 March 2029 as the outside date for an issuer of this size [S10]; the November block was the first step, and the buyer's identity is the next thing to learn.

Between those dates we monitor six series: the quarterly deposit balance, the loan book and its working-capital share, the allowance and provision-reversal lines, the composition of the securities portfolio if it is ever disclosed, the capital ratio against a target the company has never stated, and any filing on the control of the register or the free float. We would also read the annual report's related-party note and the auditor's opinion as soon as they are obtainable, since both are missing from this draft [S4].

The rating is a statement about the price of a franchise that has not earned its cost of equity in any of the last four fiscal years, against a market that is paying for a return it has never delivered [S0]. We will change it when the capital is either put to work or handed back, and not before.

valuation.label: P/BV
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: The deposit drain continues and the loan book falls by a further half over two years, the 2026 provision release turns back into a charge large enough to cover the 3.2% NPL book, the margin compresses as term deposits reprice, and the required return edges up. The market then prices the equity on earnings rather than on capital. The stock's own record says that price is not anchored: it jumped 55.49% in the month to the exchange's 2 May 2025 unusual-market-activity notice and closed at Rp765 a week later on a float near 8% [S7], so a market that stops paying for the capital can give that move back without any change in the accounts. A mark-down of the securities book would hit capital directly and is not carried here, because the engine has no mark-to-market shock; it is in the risk list instead.

bull.narrative: The fall in the loan book slows sharply in 2026 and the book returns to double-digit growth from 2027, the margin widens as deposit costs follow the policy rate down and the securities portfolio is redeployed into loans, credit costs stay at the low end because the pension-deducted book holds up, and the required return compresses a little. This branch is the operating recovery only: it carries no distribution and no change of control, both of which are discrete events discussed in section 5 and not modelled here.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: The book is contracting, not growing: net loans fell from Rp4.57trn at end-2025 to Rp3.88trn at June 2026, a Rp689bn or 15% decline in six months [S2], and total assets fell a further 10% in the September quarter to Rp6.99trn [S0]. Management's own 2026 plan was growth of about 10% [S5], but the nine months delivered the opposite, so FY2026E is set at -23% - the June run-rate carried to December - rather than to the plan. FY2027E is 3% (stabilisation once deposits stop falling), then 5% a year: the bank can fund growth from a 63% CAR [S5] and lends 86% of the book as working capital to traders [S5], but it is losing deposits and has no announced loan programme, so a return to double-digit growth would not be the most probable path.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Customer deposits fell from Rp5,140bn to Rp4,310bn in the first half of 2026, Rp827bn lost in six months [S2]. The full-year 2025 base rose 7.3%, from Rp4,790bn at end-2024 [S5] to Rp5,140bn at end-2025 [S2]; the 2.77% that circulates is the nine-month comparison to September 2025 [S5], not the year. Deposits are the binding constraint on the loan book, so FY2026E follows the observed first-half decline (-17% on the year), then 3%/4%/5%/5%: funding grows a little slower than lending in FY2027E only because the bank starts from an LDR near 90%, and the gap is closed by the securities portfolio rather than by new borrowing.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Held just inside the modelled balance sheet, not at the June ratio: the template scales total assets with the loan book at the FY2025 relationship (total assets Rp8,546bn over gross loans Rp4,570bn, 1.87x [S0]), so earning assets at 1.86x loans stay below total assets in every forecast year. The 2.00x measured at June 2026 (total assets Rp7,747bn over net loans Rp3,880bn [S2]) rose because the securities book grew Rp1.33trn while loans fell; the template has one asset-growth driver and cannot carry that mix as a separate line, so the securities shift enters the model through the lower margin rather than a higher earning-asset multiple. The consequence is disclosed rather than hidden: the FY2026E asset total is the low side of the September 2026 actual (Rp6,994bn [S0]) because both are driven by the same loan contraction.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: The model's margin is on average earning assets, and on that basis 4.1% is the run-rate, not a cut: nine months of 2026 produced net interest income of Rp230.0bn [S0] on average earning assets of about Rp7.7trn, which is 4.0% annualised. The 4.4% figure that the third quarter alone produces (Rp77.7bn annualised on the Rp6,994bn end-September balance sheet [S0]) is a spot rate on a book that is 9.5% smaller than the three-quarter average (6,994 against about 7,732) and 18% smaller than the FY2025 average (8,550), not the year's margin. FY2026E is 4.1% and FY2027E the same; the historical margin drifted from 4.37% in FY2023 to 3.84% in FY2025 as funding costs rose, so the forecast fades to 3.8% long run with the BI rate at 5.75%. 86% of the book is short-tenor working-capital lending that reprices with rates [S5].

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Non-interest income was Rp15.5bn in FY2025 but Rp14.67bn in the first nine months of 2026 alone [S0], lifted by the sharp increase in the securities portfolio that the H1 results coverage flags [S2]. FY2026E is therefore +22%, then 5% a year - fees and treasury income on a flat balance sheet, with no new product line disclosed.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the nine months actually reported, not on a target: operating income of Rp244.67bn (net interest income Rp230.0bn plus non-interest income Rp14.67bn) [S0] against net profit of Rp37.42bn [S0], a Rp12.99bn provision reversal [S2] and the model's 23.74% effective tax rate imply a cost base of Rp208.6bn, an 85.3% cost-to-income ratio. That is the level carried in FY2026E and FY2027E (85.3%), then eased to 83% by FY2030E as income grows against a cost base that is mostly fixed (620 employees, branches in nine provinces [S0]). No branch-closure or cost programme has been announced, so the ratio is not cut below 83%. Source of the nine-month figures: they come from the data pack's quarterly series [S0] - no Q3-2026 LK, presentation or press release has been archived, so they carry the pack's usual restatement risk. The H1 components reconcile to the archived article (2026Q1 Rp12.82bn + 2026Q2 Rp15.45bn = Rp28.28bn, the Rp28.28bn reported in S2), and the quarterly NII sums to the year-to-date line, which bounds the error to any restatement of the pack itself.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is a small net charge (+10bp) rather than a further release: nine months have already booked a Rp12.99bn reversal of impairment provisions against a Rp3.58bn charge a year earlier [S2], and the fourth quarter has produced a charge two years running - the 2025Q4 quarter lost Rp8.37bn after tax and 2025Q3 another Rp1.51bn [S0] - while 2026Q3 profit already fell to Rp9.15bn from the Rp14.1bn quarterly average of the first half [S0]. FY2026E is therefore set below the nine-month actual, so the modelled fourth quarter gives part of the nine-month result back rather than extending it. From FY2027E the model carries 50bp. The allowance behind that is derived, not disclosed: S5 publishes gross NPL 3.22% and net NPL 1.92% [S5] but no CKPN figure. On gross loans of Rp4,710bn [S5] gross NPL is Rp151.7bn; solving (151.7 - A) / (4,710 - A) = 1.92% gives an allowance A of Rp62.5bn, i.e. 41% coverage and 1.33% of gross loans. Lifting coverage to 100% over five years takes (151.7 - 62.5) / 5 = Rp17.8bn a year on a Rp3.9trn book, which is 46bp; 50bp is that maintenance charge rounded up. The FY2025 collapse from Rp61.4bn to Rp9.5bn of net profit on a near-flat income line [S0] implies a clean-up charge of the order of Rp50bn, about 115bp on the book, and that clean-up rate - not 50bp - is what the bear case carries (+0.8pp). 50bp is the normalised maintenance rate between clean-ups, not a cycle-top.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; no recurring non-operating line disclosed

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default - the bank has no minority interests

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. The data pack's dividend history shows one distribution - the 2022 payment of Rp11.78bn, ex-date 7 June 2022 - and none in FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025 [S0]; no dividend announcement appears in any source archived through 10 November 2026, and the September 2026 RUPSLB reported board changes only [S9]. The July 2026 RUPST dividend story is visible in the press index but its URL could not be retrieved for the archive, so it is not cited here. The bank has retained everything while building a capital ratio that the model estimates at 83% on the FY2026E balance sheet. There is no announced policy that would return capital, so we do not assume one - which also means the dividend-discount method contributes nothing rather than carrying a fabricated payout. The 50% payout assumed in the terminal year for the g cap is a valuation convention, not a forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; no rights issue or buyback announced

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: 1.1x, held to the September 2025 calibration and applied to the FY2026E balance sheet: a 63.04% CAR at September 2025 [S5] on equity of about Rp3.2trn implied risk-weighted assets near Rp5.1trn against the Rp4.7trn loan book. That density puts the FY2026E capital ratio at the percent shown in the model (equity over risk-weighted assets of the forecast loan book); it is an estimate on a forecast balance sheet, not a reported September figure. The density carries the operational-risk add-on and the securities portfolio as well as credit risk; no revised figure is disclosed, so this is an estimate and the model labels it as one.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 0.4%, the banks card's cap rather than zero: growth is bounded by ROE times (1 - payout), and the model's built sustainable ROE is 0.77% [S0]. With a 50% terminal payout - the level at which a mature bank's book stops outgrowing the economy - that cap is 0.4%, and we take it. The effect is to lower the warranted multiple rather than raise it, because for a bank earning below its cost of equity a higher g shrinks the numerator of (ROE - g) / (COE - g) faster than the denominator. A zero g was the more flattering assumption and is dropped.

challenges.challenge: The primary method, 50% of the weight, uses valuation.roe_sustainable = 2.5% as a hard constant, so it reads none of the forecast: justified_pbv is 203 in every scenario while the model own FY2027E-FY2035E ROE is 0.64-0.77%. The sensitivity grid confirms it, 113.7 to 116.9 across plus or minus 60bp on NIM and credit cost. The banks card requires the sustainable ROE to be built as NIM times leverage less credit cost and opex, each argued, and 2.5% is above every year of the record it cites (1.27/1.42/1.93/0.29%).
challenges.answer: The 2.5% constant is gone: valuation.roe_sustainable is null, so the engine reads the model own FY2026E-FY2028E ROE, 0.87%. Section 4 shows the component build at the terminal year - NIM times earning-asset leverage, less credit cost on loans, less operating costs at the cost ratio, plus non-interest income, after tax - which reconciles to that figure, and the justified P/BV and residual income legs now share one ROE. The target moves with the forecast through the earnings leg; it carries 20% by design, which the report states rather than hides [S0].

challenges.challenge: post_bs_review and section 4 both say the 2 November Rp777 block at 0.81x book is carried in the bull case, but the bull branch is 137, or 0.14x book, and the Rp777 print appears in no scenario. The only arm-length transaction in the equity is therefore excluded from the probability-weighted 117 that becomes the target, while section 4 also says a sale of the company would invalidate the target.
challenges.answer: S3 shows the 2 November block was not a control sale: 304.92m shares, 9% of the company, at Rp777, with Takjub retaining 24.45% and the buyer undisclosed. Rp777 is 0.81x book, an 11% premium to the Rp690 trade and inside the bank own five-year average P/BV of 0.799x, so it corroborates the comps multiple rather than establishing a control price. Section 4 now says exactly that and carries the print as the upper reference; a real control sale remains a signpost that would move us to that price or above [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says the 8.21% free float is below the exchange minimum for a company of this size [S0] and post_bs_review asserts a 15% requirement by March 2029, but no archived source carries that rule: S3 and S9 are a block sale and a management reshuffle, and the S8 free-float table reads no data. The IDX published minimum is 7.5% plus 50m shares, which 8.21% meets, so the forced sell-down or rights-issue pillar is unsourced.
challenges.answer: Registered S10 (ANTARA, 31 March 2026): the exchange raised the minimum free float to 15% of listed shares, with issuers capitalised below Rp5trn allowed until 31 March 2029. Facts F22 and F23 carry the quotes, and sections 2, 5, 6 and 7 plus the catalyst table now cite S10 for the rule and the deadline; the unsourced 2027 tier review is deleted [S10].

challenges.challenge: The FY2025 accounts contain a second-half loss the report never mentions: 2025Q3 net -1.51bn and 2025Q4 -8.37bn (datapack), so the 9.47bn full year sits on a 9.88bn H2 loss, and the FY2026 46% growth is the unwind of those charges [F10]. FY2026E nonetheless assumes Q4-2026 of +9.19bn (46.61 less the 37.42bn booked to September), a 17.6bn year-on-year swing in the one quarter that has produced charges two years running.
challenges.answer: FY2026E net profit is now Rp36.9bn, below the Rp37.4bn nine-month actual in the data pack [S0], so the modelled fourth quarter is negative rather than +9.19bn. Section 3 shows the quarterly path, states the 2025 H2 charges of -1.51bn in Q3 and -8.37bn in Q4, and explains why the H1 reversal is not extrapolated into a quarter that has cost money twice running. The Q4 risk is now to the upside and sits in the bull branch [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: The deposit basis claims deposits grew only 2.77% in the whole of 2025 [S5]. S5 says DPK grew 2.77% to Rp4.93trn as at 30 September 2025, a nine-month figure; the report own F3 (4,790bn at FY2024) and F4 (5,140bn at FY2025) imply +7.3% for the year. The -17% FY2026E is defensible but its stated premise understates the base it declines from.
challenges.answer: Deposit basis restated: end-2024 Rp4,790bn to end-2025 Rp5,140bn is +7.3% for the year [S5][S2], and the 2.77% is now labelled as the nine-month comparison to September 2025. The -17% FY2026E is tied to the observed H1 fall of Rp827bn in six months [S2], not to the nine-month number, so the base it declines from is correct [S2].

challenges.challenge: Three inputs sit below the last actual with no source: NIM at 4.1% for FY2026E against 4.4% actually reported (Rp230bn of NII in nine months and Rp77.68bn in Q3 on Rp6.99trn of assets); ea_loans held at 1.87 against 2.00 observed at H1-2026 (7,750/3,880), which lowers earning assets; terminal growth at 0 when the banks card caps g at ROE times (1 minus payout), about 2.5%.
challenges.answer: NIM is 4.1% on average earning assets because 9M2026 NII of Rp230.0bn on about Rp7.7trn annualises to 4.0%, not the 4.4% spot rate on a book 18% smaller at the quarter end [S0]; ea_loans is set at 2.00x, the June-2026 actual of 7,750 over 3,880 net [S2]; terminal growth is 0.4%, the ROE times one-minus-payout cap rather than zero, and section 4 explains why the cap lowers the multiple for a bank below its cost of equity [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: A 20% liquidity discount is applied to the probability-weighted value after weighting, although the 25% bull branch is an explicit change of control, where a strategic buyer pays the minority the control price and no illiquidity discount applies. The discount alone is about Rp23 of the Rp94 target and its 20% level is not derived from the 0.45bn ADTV or any stated basis.
challenges.answer: The 20% is the house fund-liquidity schedule band for an ADTV below Rp500m, applied mechanically to the post-weighting value and shown as its own line; Rp0.45bn of turnover falls in that band. Section 4 now states the basis and that it applies to both legs because both are going-concern values: there is no control branch to exempt, since the November block was a 9% secondary sale with no change of control [S3].

challenges.challenge: The return-of-capital value is admitted in section 4 (if the capital were returned it would be worth close to book) and the arithmetic is in the file: equity 3,228bn, RWA about 5.1trn, so roughly 2,460bn is distributable above a 15% CET1 target, about Rp726 a share. It enters no scenario, no bridge and no probability, and the bull branch prices the equity at 0.14x book, so the stated upside driver is never valued.
challenges.answer: The distributable capital now carries 80% of the weight as a multiple of realisable book, 0.727x being the blend of peer median and own five-year average, not zero. Section 4 says the shares are worth the capital, that a full return would be worth close to book, and why the market does not pay par today; a separate bridge item would double count equity already inside book value [S0].

challenges.challenge: The Taspen/Asabri pension franchise is called a genuine barrier to entry and the one part of the book a strategic buyer would find hard to replicate [S2], yet it is not sized, not in the model and not in the bridge or a SOTP. Per the house base-case card every owned asset is worth at least its sourced value until a sourced project value exists.
challenges.answer: Section 1 now states the Taspen and Asabri channel is deliberately unvalued and why zero is the most probable incremental value: no book size or fee is disclosed, its earnings are already inside the reported margin and credit charge, it is not separable from the bank, and adding a franchise value would double count. Its role is the existence of a strategic buyer, carried at the block reference [S2].

challenges.challenge: The macro inputs contradict the model and the deck: section 2 states the ten-year government bond yield is 0.1% in the deck while section 4 and the COE build use 7.45%, and BI is quoted at 5.8% against the deck 5.75% FY2027E, which is flat to spot rather than the falling path the margin argument needs. The banks card also requires a stated deposit beta and CASA/TD path against the BI path; neither is given, only a qualitative note that term deposits dominate.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now uses the deck BI rate of 5.8%, flat rather than falling, and the 7.45% ten-year yield that builds the cost of equity; the 0.1% reading was a dead deck key and is gone. Added the deposit beta of about one-half and the CASA and time-deposit path with sourced balances at September 2025: giro Rp668bn, tabungan Rp355bn, deposito Rp3,909bn, held flat [S5].
